lessons.title: Roles and boundaries
lessons.why: A request lands on you not because it's yours, but because you're the closest person to the data. Half of an analyst's "urgent" tasks belong to someone else: a broken pipeline, a process that needs rebuilding, a forecast that needs an uncertainty estimate. Being able to name the task's actual owner isn't a way to dodge it — it's a way to make sure it actually gets solved.
lessons.form:
DE  — getting the data there: pipelines, storage, input quality
DA  — what happened and why: a one-off analysis, an answer to a question
BI  — regular reporting: marts, dashboards, metrics
BA  — processes and requirements: how the work is structured and what to change
DS  — forecasting and probability: models, experiments
lessons.example:
"The dashboard breaks every morning, the data is from yesterday"
  → DE territory: the nightly pipeline didn't land

"Why did sales drop in Kansai?"
  → DA territory: a one-off analysis with a conclusion

"I need this report every Monday at 9:00"
  → BI territory: regularity turns an analysis into a product
lessons.reads: The same question — "what's going on with sales" — can turn out to be any of the three tasks. What tells them apart isn't the topic or the difficulty, but what happens to the answer: is it looked at once, looked at every week, or does the source need fixing.
lessons.wrong:
"The dashboard breaks every morning"
  → the analyst manually re-runs the export every morning
lessons.wrongWhy: The task gets solved and stays unsolved at the same time: the numbers are there, but the cause — a broken pipeline — is still there too. A month later this is a daily forty-minute ritual that nobody counts as work and that the person who could actually fix it never sees. Manually working around someone else's outage is the most expensive kind of help: it masks the problem just enough for people to stop noticing it.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask yourself: if I fix this right now, does the problem disappear — or come back tomorrow in the same shape? If it comes back, you're treating a symptom in someone else's territory, and that needs to be said out loud, not quietly patched over by re-running an export.

lessons.title: From "build me a dashboard" to a brief
lessons.why: "Build me a sales dashboard" isn't a task, it's a direction. It's missing the one thing that matters: what decision will this person make after looking at the result? Without that you'll build something technically flawless that nobody needs — and find out a month later, when nobody opens the dashboard.
lessons.form:
What to find out before starting work:
  Decision   — what will you do once you see the answer?
  Recipient  — who else looks at this, and why?
  Cut        — what are we comparing by: period, brand, region?
  Deadline   — when is it needed, and what happens if it's late?
  Done       — what signal tells us the task is closed?
lessons.example:
Request:   "Need a sales dashboard"
Asked:     "What will you decide by looking at it?"
Answer:    "Where to send the field team next month"

Became:    top 10 outlets with sales down more than 20%
           vs. last month, with the sales rep's contact.
           Viewed by the field team lead, once a month.
lessons.reads: One question about the decision compressed an endless "sales dashboard" into a ten-row table that takes an hour to build and will actually get used.
lessons.wrong:
Request:  "Need a sales dashboard"
Built:    20 charts — revenue, units, average price,
          trend, shares, region map, top lists, funnel
Outcome:  the stakeholder opened it once and asked:
          "Where do I see where to go?"
lessons.wrongWhy: A "one for everything" dashboard is an attempt to guess the question instead of asking it. It's more expensive to build, slower to run, needs upkeep, and still doesn't answer the stakeholder's actual question — it drowns among twenty charts, nineteen of which aren't about it. Completeness works against clarity here.
lessons.selfCheck: Before opening the editor, finish this sentence: "The stakeholder will look at this and decide ___." If you can't finish it, the task isn't defined yet, and it's too early to start.

lessons.title: Defining a metric
lessons.why: Two reports about the same thing almost never diverge because of a query bug — they diverge because "active outlet" or "revenue" meant something different to each author. An argument over whose numbers are right eats up the whole meeting and goes nowhere: both sides computed correctly, just different things.
lessons.form:
A metric definition has five parts:
  Source        — which table, over what period
  Filters       — what's included
  Exclusions    — what's deliberately dropped, and why
  Granularity   — what does one result row represent
  Formula       — exactly how it's computed
lessons.example:
Monthly active outlet:
  Source:       fact_sellout, month by week_start
  Filters:      customer_type <> 'distributor'
  Exclusions:   returns (units < 0) not counted
  Granularity:  one row — one customer_id per month
  Formula:      COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) where SUM(units) > 0
lessons.reads: A definition two people can apply independently and get the same number from. Each item closes off a specific argument that would otherwise happen later, in front of an audience.
lessons.wrong: An active outlet is one that had sales.
lessons.wrongWhy: Sounds complete and answers not a single practical question. Sales over what period — a month, a quarter, any period ever? Does a distributor count as an outlet? An outlet that sold one unit and took back a return of two — active or not? Everyone will compute it their own way and be sure they did the obvious thing.
lessons.selfCheck: Hand the definition to a colleague and ask them to compute it without asking you any questions. If they ask one, that's the item missing from the definition.

lessons.title: Checks before you send it
lessons.why: A mistake found by the recipient can't be "just fixed": along with that one number, they stop trusting all your other numbers too, including the correct ones. Five minutes of checking before you send it is cheaper than a month spent rebuilding trust in the report.
lessons.form:
Four checks before sending:
  Total       — does the sum reconcile with the source or last report?
  Order       — is the number plausible in scale for this business?
  Completeness — are all periods and entities present, no gaps?
  Extremes    — what's in the largest and smallest row?
lessons.example:
Report: 2025 sales by month

  Total        51,534K ¥ — reconciled against the annual P&L, matches
  Order        ~4.3M per month — in line with last year
  Completeness 12 rows, all months present
  Extremes     max — December (peak), min — February (short month)
lessons.reads: None of the four checks requires recomputing anything. All of them are about looking at your own result through the eyes of someone who knows the business, not the query.
lessons.wrong:
Report: 2025 sales by month
Rows in result: 11
lessons.wrongWhy: Eleven months instead of twelve is the most common and least noticeable mistake: a month dropped out because of a filter boundary or a gap in the data, while the total still looks perfectly normal and gives no sign of anything wrong. There's exactly one way to catch it — deliberately counting the rows and comparing against how many there should be.
lessons.selfCheck: Before sending, answer out loud: "If this number is wrong, how exactly will I find out?" No answer means there was no check — just a feeling that everything was fine.

lessons.title: The value chain
lessons.why: Data doesn't fall from the sky: every row is born at a specific link in the chain — someone shipped it, someone received it, someone rang it up. Without understanding exactly where a row originated, you can't answer the main question about any data: what it doesn't and can't contain.
lessons.form:
Manufacturer → Distributor → Point of sale → Buyer
      │              │               │             │
   sell-in       stock on hand    sell-out     invisible
 fact_sellin    fact_stock     fact_sellout       —
lessons.example:
"How much did we sell in June?" — three different answers:

  shipped to distributors    fact_sellin
  sitting on their shelves   fact_stock
  bought at outlets          fact_sellout

The numbers don't match, and shouldn't: they're three different events.
lessons.reads: "Sold" without naming the link isn't a metric — it's the start of a conversation.
lessons.wrong:
"How much of our product did consumers buy in Saitama?"
  → SUM(units) from fact_sellout for Saitama
lessons.wrongWhy: The query answers a different question: how much moved through the registers of the outlets that made it into our records. A buyer could have bought from a competing distributor, at a chain that doesn't share data, or on a marketplace. Sell-out isn't "the market" — it's "the part of the market visible to us", and the gap grows the lower our coverage is.
lessons.selfCheck: Before answering a question about sales, name the link: shipment, warehouse, or register. Didn't name it — you're counting something unknown.

lessons.title: Order-to-cash
lessons.why: "Sold" isn't one event — it's a chain of statuses: order placed, reserved, shipped, delivered, received, invoiced, paid. Two sales reports built on different statuses will produce different numbers — and both authors will be sure they computed the same thing.
lessons.form:
Order → Reserve → Shipment → Delivery → Receipt → Invoice → Payment

  Revenue      — at transfer of control over the goods: shipment
                 or receipt, depending on what the contract says
  Receivables  — invoiced, money not in yet
  Cash         — money landed in the account
lessons.example:
"How much did we sell in March?" — three honest numbers:

  Orders placed        4,910K ¥   sales funnel
  Shipped               4,694K ¥   revenue
  Landed in the account 3,380K ¥   cash, some on payment terms
lessons.reads: Three numbers for the same month diverge by a quarter, and all three are correct. Which one is "sales" isn't up to the analyst — it's up to the stakeholder's question.
lessons.wrong:
Report "March sales" — 4,910K ¥
(taken from order date, because it was easiest)
lessons.wrongWhy: An order is intent, not a sale: some get canceled, some ship in April, some get cut down by stock availability. A report by order date systematically overstates and reconciles with neither accounting nor shipments, and the gap grows toward month-end, when orders get stockpiled ahead of time.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask: which date is a row dated to — order, shipment, or payment? If a report says "sales" but has no answer to that, it isn't finished yet.

lessons.title: Sell-in and sell-out
lessons.why: Sell-in is what you shipped into the channel; sell-out is what the channel sold onward. The company earns on the first, but lives on the second: if the product doesn't leave the shelf, there's no next order. A report that treats these words as synonyms sooner or later leads to a decision based on someone else's warehouse instead of actual demand.
lessons.form:
sell-in   manufacturer → distributor    fact_sellin
sell-out  outlet → buyer                fact_sellout

ratio = sell-in / sell-out

  ≈ 1   channel stock is stable
  > 1   channel is overstocking
  < 1   channel is drawing down stock
lessons.example:
Sell-in to sell-out ratio, Q4 2025:

  «Setouchi Trading» LLC        28,203 / 11,574 = 2.44
  «Hokuriku Supply» JSC            9,216 /  8,760 = 1.05
  «Hokusei Trading» LLC           12,018 / 11,509 = 1.04
  «Tokai Group» LLC     10,038 /  9,640 = 1.04
  ... the other eight              1.04 to 1.05
lessons.reads: Eleven distributors out of twelve stay close to one — that's the channel working normally. One stands out at double: it took in 2.44 times more than the outlets it serves actually sold.
lessons.wrong: "Sales grew 20%" — computed from sell-in
lessons.wrongWhy: Growing shipments can mean anything: real demand growth, a one-off purchase to hit an annual bonus, gearing up for a promo, or a distributor's planning mistake. The only way to tell them apart is sell-out — and if it didn't grow, "sales growth" means the product just moved from your warehouse to someone else's, and it'll come back as a drop next quarter.
lessons.selfCheck: Hearing "sales grew", ask: into the channel, or out of it? If only into it, check inventory levels before celebrating.

lessons.title: S&OP and demand forecasting
lessons.why: Planning is the one process where analytics moves money directly: a demand forecast grows into a production, purchasing, and shipment plan, and a mistake turns into either a shortage or stock that later gets written off. The analyst here isn't decorating someone else's numbers with a chart — they're on the hook for whether the number can be trusted.
lessons.form:
Demand forecast   how much will sell — an estimate, built bottom-up
      ↓
Sales plan        how much we'll ship — a target, set top-down
      ↓
Production and purchasing plan

Gap "plan − forecast" = a decision to load the channel.
It has to be named out loud, not appear on its own.
lessons.example:
April, «Fruvia» brand:

  Demand forecast   18,200 units   estimated to sell
  Sales plan        22,000 units   committed to ship
  Gap                3,800 units   will sit in channel stock

Reason for the gap on record: entering a new chain on May 1.
lessons.reads: A forecast and a plan don't have to match — but the difference between them has to have a name. Here it does, so the April surplus sitting in warehouses won't be a surprise in June.
lessons.wrong:
Demand forecast   18,200 units
Sales plan        22,000 units
Reason for the gap: not discussed
lessons.wrongWhy: Without a named reason, the gap doesn't disappear — it just stops being visible: those 3,800 units still end up in the channel's warehouses. A quarter later they'll show up as a drop in orders, and it'll get pinned on sales, not planning — because by then nobody will remember there was nothing to overperform against.
lessons.selfCheck: Find where the plan diverges from the forecast and ask what justifies the difference. An answer of "that's just what was decided" means the decision was made but never recorded — and there'll be nothing to deliberately repeat next cycle.

lessons.title: Seasonality and period comparison
lessons.why: For a seasonal product, comparing against last month measures the calendar, not the business: water sales climb toward summer, vitamins toward autumn, and that happens regardless of what the company did. A month-over-month report on a category like that regularly produces conclusions and budget decisions that are exactly backwards.
lessons.form:
Ways to compare a period:

  MoM   vs. the previous month      seasonality NOT removed
  YoY   vs. the same month          seasonality removed, but noisy
        last year
  YTD   since the start of the year  stabilizes toward December
  MAT   trailing 12 months vs.       seasonality fully removed,
        the prior 12                 refreshes every month
lessons.example:
«Vitanor» brand, the same growth, three answers:

  August → September 2025      282 → 1,174    +316%
  September 2024 → 2025        862 → 1,174     +36%
  Year 2024 → 2025           9,126 → 9,419     +3.2%
lessons.reads: Three correct numbers about one brand, a hundredfold apart. +316% is the move from the summer trough to the autumn peak, and it repeats every year. Only the last line answers how the brand is actually growing.
lessons.wrong: "Vitamins grew 316% — let's shift budget there"
lessons.wrongWhy: In 2024 the same August-to-September transition produced +79% (481 → 862) — that's seasonality, not an achievement. A decision made on MoM in a seasonal category buys the season at the price of "growth": the budget arrives at the peak and sits idle once the season turns.
lessons.selfCheck: Before comparing periods, ask: does this category have a season? If yes, compare against the same period last year or a rolling year, and never against the previous month.

lessons.title: Distribution and shelf presence
lessons.why: A brand's sales are the product of two things: how many outlets carry it, and how fast it moves off the shelf there. Distribution accounts for the first half, and it's the only part the company controls directly with its own hands. A brand with no distribution doesn't lose to the buyer — it simply never meets them, and no amount of advertising fixes that.
lessons.form:
numeric (ND)    share of outlets that carry the brand
                counts addresses

weighted (WD)   share of those outlets' turnover in channel
                turnover — counts money behind the addresses

WD > ND whenever the brand sits in larger-than-average outlets

  ND drops faster than WD  →  small outlets are dropping it
  WD drops faster than ND  →  large ones are, and that's a fire
lessons.reads: Through mid-2025, numeric distribution drops twice as fast as weighted — the brand is leaving small outlets, and the money is still mostly intact. From August, weighted collapses thirty points in five months: the wave has reached the large outlets, and that's a different stage of the problem.
lessons.wrong: "Distribution is 94%" — said without specifying which kind, or over what base
lessons.wrongWhy: Numeric and weighted for the same brand diverge here by fourteen points, and on other portfolios the gap runs as high as forty. On top of that, weighted is sometimes computed over an outlet's total turnover and sometimes over just its category turnover — again two different numbers. A target of "80% distribution" with no clarification turns into two incomparable work plans: for «Nettora», 80% weighted is reached by winning back five outlets, while 80% numeric needs forty-five.
lessons.selfCheck: On hearing a distribution number, ask twice: which kind — numeric or weighted — and weighted over what base. No answer means the number means nothing.

lessons.title: Penetration, repeat purchase, and rate of sale
lessons.why: Market share is convenient to compute as one number, but it can't be managed as one number: it's made of three independent things — how many people bought it, how many times they came back, and how much they took each time. Each is fixed by different actions, and growth in one is easily eaten by a drop in another. A report saying "share is unchanged" says nothing at all about what's actually happening to the brand without breaking it down.
lessons.form:
market share = penetration × frequency × purchase volume

  penetration     share of buyers who bought the brand at least once
  frequency       how many times those buyers repurchased
  purchase volume how much they take per purchase

The same arithmetic from outlet data:

  units = outlets × weeks with a sale × units in such a week

rate of sale = units per outlet per week
lessons.example:
Household panel, a new flavor launch:

                          before    after
  penetration               4%       11%
  purchases per buyer       3.4       1.3
  purchase size, ¥          180       185
  ───────────────────────────────────────
  market share              2.1%      2.1%
lessons.reads: Penetration grew 2.75x, frequency dropped 2.6x — the product stayed exactly in place. Lots of people tried it and almost nobody came back: the ad campaign worked, the product didn't.
lessons.wrong: "Penetration doubled — the launch is a success"
lessons.wrongWhy: Penetration shows whether the ad and sampling budget worked, and it almost always grows from that spend alone. The only honest test of the product itself is the repeat purchase: the share of triers who come back, and the time to the second purchase. Until those two are checked, "successful launch" only means "we spent the budget and got noticed", and a second ad wave will repeat the exact same cycle with the exact same money.
lessons.selfCheck: On seeing any product-of-factors metric grow, break it into its factors and check each one. If one rose and another fell, the conclusion follows the product, not the pleasant half.

lessons.title: Promo: real lift and cannibalization
lessons.why: A promo almost always produces a good-looking first number: volume during the promo week is two to three times the baseline. The problem is that number is inflated three ways at once — the discount also applied to volume that would have sold anyway, part of the growth flowed in from neighboring SKUs, and part of it was simply pulled forward from future weeks. A repeat decision made on that first number repeats the loss too.
lessons.form:
three corrections, each reducing the result:

  1  scope       measure where the promo ran, not the whole brand
  2  level       measure at the category level, not just the promo'd
                 SKU (otherwise cannibalization is invisible)
  3  horizon     before / during / after
                 (otherwise stock-up buying is invisible)

  and finally — money, not units:
  margin lift = extra volume × promo margin
              − lost margin on the baseline volume
              − promo costs
lessons.example:
«Milvara», 30% discount, weekly averages:

                    units      revenue ¥    price ¥
  4 weeks before    1,353.3     104,645      77.33
  3 weeks of promo  3,327.0     180,157      54.15
  4 weeks after     1,376.0     106,344      77.28

  units +146%, revenue +72%, price −30%
lessons.reads: Units grow twice as fast as revenue: the discount also applied to the 1,353 units a week that would have sold with no promo at all — about 94 thousand yen over three weeks. There's no post-promo dip, but that's a property of the product: nobody stocks up on yogurt.
lessons.wrong: "The promo delivered +146%" — computed on the promo'd SKU during the promo weeks
lessons.wrongWhy: This number contains none of the three corrections. It doesn't know some buyers simply switched from a neighboring flavor of the same brand; it doesn't know the category might dip below baseline after the promo; and it counts units where the decision should be made on profit. For a shelf-stable product at a deep discount, these corrections eat up half the apparent lift, and a promo reported as a 2.5x jump turns out to be unprofitable.
lessons.selfCheck: Before analyzing a promo, ask three questions: where did it run, what sat next to it on the shelf, and what happened two weeks after it ended. If even one has no data, call the result an upper-bound estimate.

lessons.title: TRx, NRx, and market share
lessons.why: In pharma, sales follow a doctor's decision, and the length of a treatment course sits between the two events. A metric that counts every prescription describes an already-accumulated patient base and is the last thing to turn around. Planning off it means building the year on inertia that runs out exactly when the current courses run out.
lessons.form:
TRx   all prescriptions for a period, including refills
      a lagging indicator, describes the base

NRx   only new starts of a drug for a patient
      a leading indicator, describes the inflow

TRx ≈ NRx × average course length

market share: compute over MAT (sum of trailing 12 months,
shifted monthly), not a single month
lessons.reads: The month-by-month share swings fourfold because the brands' seasons don't align: in the month of a competitor's peak, your share drops with not one lost pack. Over a rolling year, each brand's season enters the window exactly once, and what's left is the real movement — down three points over fifteen months.
lessons.wrong: "Share fell from 49.5% to 24.4% in a year — we're losing the market"
lessons.wrongWhy: That's comparing February to June — vitamin season against off-season — and it'll repeat next year too. In a single month, a ratio metric's numerator and denominator both jump, and for different reasons. Before explaining a share drop by your own actions, compute it over a rolling year and separately check what happened to the denominator — maybe the market itself simply grew.
lessons.selfCheck: For any market-share series, ask: what window was it computed over. If it's monthly, don't draw conclusions about the brand's position until you've seen the same series over MAT.

lessons.title: Panel data in pharma
lessons.why: A company knows its own sales exactly, but the market and its competitors only through purchased data, and that's always an estimate: a sample of pharmacies extrapolated to the whole country. Forgetting the word "estimate", an analyst starts reconciling the panel against the accounting system, arguing over missing percentage points, and drawing market conclusions from a supplier's methodology change.
lessons.form:
panel = pharmacy sample × extrapolation factor

what is comparable to what:

  our shipments  ≠  pharmacy sales   ≠  prescriptions
  (accounting       (panel,             (Rx panel,
   system)           an estimate)        an estimate)

between them stand a distributor's warehouse, a pharmacy's
warehouse, and a patient's decision

market share = our sales from the panel / market from the panel
               (numerator and denominator — one source)
lessons.example:
One drug, one quarter:

  shipments to distributors        118,000 packs
  pharmacy sales per the panel      99,000 packs (24% share)
  distributor stock growth          14,000 packs
lessons.reads: A 19,000-pack gap isn't an error: 14,000 sat down in channel stock, and the rest falls within the extrapolation margin of error. A shipment and a pharmacy purchase are different events, separated by a warehouse and by time.
lessons.wrong: "Our share = our shipments / market per the panel"
lessons.wrongWhy: The numerator and denominator are different events, measured by different sources at different points in the chain. In a quarter when the channel is building stock, this share will grow with not one extra pharmacy purchase; in a quarter of drawing that stock down, it'll fall. The numerator has to come from the same source as the denominator: our sales from the panel, not our sell-in.
lessons.selfCheck: Keep a label on every number in a market report: source and event. If you can't write "panel, pharmacy sales" or "accounting system, shipments" next to a figure, it's too early to show it.

lessons.title: Decomposing "why did it drop"
lessons.why: "Revenue fell 49%" isn't a task: it has no owner and no first step. Decomposition turns a metric's movement into factors and carries the analysis down to the link someone in the company can actually influence. Until that link is found, discussing the drop stays discussing the drop.
lessons.form:
1  pick an identity — an equality that always holds:
     revenue = outlets × revenue per outlet
     revenue = units × price
     volume  = outlets × frequency × volume per purchase

2  compute the change in each factor

3  check: the product of the relative changes
   must reproduce the observed change in the metric

4  stop at the link that has an owner
lessons.reads: The factors moved in opposite directions, and the product reconciles with the actual figure — so the breakdown is complete. The brand didn't lose demand, it lost shelf space: where it stayed, sales even grew. The task belongs to sales, not marketing.
lessons.wrong: "Revenue per outlet grew 22% — the remaining outlets are performing better"
lessons.wrongWhy: An average changes for two reasons: the members changed, or the composition of the group changed. The outlets that were lost averaged 24,738 ¥ against 29,810 ¥ for the ones that remained — their departure alone lifts the average by 11%. The 33 comparable outlets only grew 9.7%. A metric that improves from losing small outlets is doubly dangerous: put into a KPI, it turns shrinking distribution into apparent gains in efficiency.
lessons.selfCheck: After decomposing, ask two questions: does the product of the factors reconcile with the fact, and who will you hand the result to. No owner means the analysis isn't finished; no reconciliation means the breakdown is wrong.

lessons.title: ABC-XYZ segmentation
lessons.why: There's always less attention and warehouse space than there are assortment items, and splitting them evenly is the most expensive approach possible. ABC tells you how costly a mistake on an item is; XYZ tells you how likely it is. Together they answer where a person is needed, where an automatic rule is enough, and where an item doesn't earn the effort at all.
lessons.form:
ABC  by contribution to revenue or margin
     A — up to 80% cumulative share, B — up to 95%, C — the tail
     the thresholds are a convention, not a law

XYZ  by demand stability, usually via the
     coefficient of variation CV = σ / mean

  AX  auto-order, precise stock calculation
  AZ  manual attention and safety stock — put effort here
  CX  a simple replenishment rule
  CZ  order to demand, or a question about delisting
lessons.example:
29 SKUs in an FMCG division, 12 months:

  rank    SKU share   cumulative revenue share
     6       21%             36.3%
    19       66%             79.5%
    20       69%             82.2%

  largest SKU — 8.5% of revenue, smallest — 1.0%
lessons.reads: The 20/80 rule doesn't hold here: the top fifth of the assortment delivers 36%, and reaching 80% takes all the way to SKU 20 out of 29. The assortment is even — there's no easy "ballast" to cut.
lessons.wrong: "Demand for this SKU is unstable: CV 35%, raise the safety stock"
lessons.wrongWhy: The coefficient of variation measures spread, not unpredictability, and it can't tell a regular seasonal wave or the brand's own promo apart from real chaos. A seasonal water and a snack with a spike in its promo month both get a high CV, even though both events are known well in advance — one from nature's calendar, the other from trade marketing's. Before running XYZ, the series is cleaned: strip out the season, break out the promo as a separate effect, and compute variation on what's left.
lessons.selfCheck: Before computing CV, look at the series with your own eyes. If a spike is explained by the calendar — a season or your own promo — it isn't uncertainty, and a safety stock won't fix it.

lessons.title: Correlation and causation
lessons.why: Decisions are made on the basis of causes: if A causes B, you can influence B through A. Correlation says only that the series move together, and it's routinely mistaken for a cause — after which the company spends budget on a link that doesn't exist.
lessons.form:
Three explanations for any correlation besides "A causes B":

  common factor  one cause lifts both A and B
                 (season, inflation, market growth)
  reverse        B actually causes A
  selection      the objects didn't enter the groups
                 at random, and differed before
                 the measurement

What raises confidence in a causal link:
  a control group — same period, no treatment
  a mechanism — an account of how A affects B
  the link survives removal of the common factor
lessons.example:
Water and juice sales, 2025:

  correlation of monthly sales                   0.84
  correlation of year-over-year changes           0.10

Removing the season kills the link — so there wasn't one:
a common factor was lifting both series at once.
lessons.reads: The first number describes a shared wave, not a link between the brands. The second is what's left of the link once the wave is taken out: essentially nothing. Shelving them together would produce a coincidence, not growth.
lessons.wrong: "Correlation 0.84 — the juice pulls the water, let's shelve them as a pair"
lessons.wrongWhy: Correlation is symmetric: swap the series and you get the same number, so it contains no direction whatsoever. Nor does the size of the coefficient help: 0.84 is just as compatible with a shared season as with a real link. The only way to tell them apart is a test — remove the suspected common factor and see what's left.
lessons.selfCheck: Before concluding "A affects B," answer three questions: what third factor could have lifted both, could the arrow point the other way, how did the objects end up in the groups being compared. If even one has no answer, you have an observation, not a cause.

lessons.title: Conclusion first
lessons.why: A report exists so that someone can make a decision. The reader goes from "what does this mean for me" to "how do we know," not the other way around — and if there's no conclusion in the first two lines, they read no further, and the work turns into a file in an attachment.
lessons.form:
Four parts of the opening paragraph:

  conclusion     one sentence the reader can
                 retell to a third person
  support        the minimum numbers that prove it
  recommendation what you advise doing
  request        what you need from the reader: a decision,
                 budget, sign-off — or an explicit "nothing"

Uncertainty is split into three levels:
  what's confirmed · what's in question · what I'll check and when
lessons.example:
Bad: "Sending over the analysis of the brand's decline.
Attached is the extract by outlet, channel and region."

Good: "The brand lost half its revenue purely by going off
the shelf: we are no longer stocked in 46 of 79 outlets, and
where we remain we sell 22% more. I suggest starting with the
five largest outlets. I need a decision on the negotiation
budget."
lessons.reads: The second version can be read on a phone between meetings and decided on without opening the attachment. Its numbers are selected to fit the conclusion: of the analysis's four pairs of figures, two remain — the ones that prove the shelf was lost.
lessons.wrong:
"Revenue was 1 079 055 ¥ against 2 121 702 ¥. Outlets: 33
against 79. Revenue per outlet: 32 699 ¥ against 26 857 ¥."
lessons.wrongWhy: These are facts with no conclusion, and they look conscientious: "I'm not imposing an interpretation." In practice you're handing the reader back work you've already done — running the decomposition and seeing which multiplier moved. They have neither the time nor the context of the calculation, so most often they'll do nothing.
lessons.selfCheck: Cover everything but the first two lines and ask: what will a person do having read only this? If the answer is "open the attachment," the paragraph isn't written yet.

lessons.title: Choosing a chart
lessons.why: A chart doesn't illustrate the text, it answers a question faster than a table can. A form that doesn't match the question isn't merely awkward — it hands the reader a different conclusion, and that's what they'll carry away, not the caption underneath.
lessons.form:
The question determines the form:

  change over time            a line
  comparison across           bars, sorted
  categories                  by size
  relationship between two    a scatter plot
  quantities
  contribution to a change    a waterfall
  accumulation to a threshold Pareto: bars + a curve
  shares of one whole (3–5)   a stacked bar, not a pie

Axis: bars start at zero, always — length encodes magnitude.
On a line truncation is allowed, but a scale break gets labeled.
lessons.example:
Question: how dependent is the company on a few products?

  SKUs in FMCG in total                        29
  the top 20% of SKUs give                  36.3% of revenue
  reaching 80% of revenue takes         20 SKUs of 29

Form: Pareto — descending bars plus a cumulative curve.
lessons.reads: The cumulative curve gives the answer at a glance: the top is modest, the tail is long, concentration is moderate. A pie with 29 sectors doesn't answer this question at all — summing angles by eye is impossible.
lessons.wrong:
Growth of 3.2% over a year, drawn as bars with the axis
starting at the minimum: the last bar is three times the first.
lessons.wrongWhy: A bar encodes magnitude with length, so a truncated axis changes not the styling but the message itself: the ratio of lengths stops matching the ratio of numbers. An honest "+3.2%" caption doesn't save it — a picture is read instantly and whole, the number only if you linger, and what stays in memory is the surge.
lessons.selfCheck: Cover the labels and look at the geometry alone: what will a person conclude? If it diverges from the number, the form or the scale was chosen wrongly.

lessons.title: Data you're accountable for
lessons.why: A number that several departments use has a life beyond your request: it gets compared across reports, recomputed a year later, passed outside. Without rules each of those actions quietly breaks, and it's discovered in a meeting.
lessons.form:
Three questions to ask of any metric:

  definition   what exactly it counts, who owns its
               meaning, where that's written down
  historicity  does the attribute change over time, and is
               the past computed with what was true then
  access       which fields the task needs, who authorizes,
               through which channel it travels

A metric's name must reflect its definition:
  "revenue" — bad · "retail revenue (sell-out)" — good
lessons.example:
Revenue for 2025 — three correct numbers:

  sales        51 533 887 ¥   at retail (sell-out)
  commercial   42 713 947 ¥   shipments before discounts
  finance      39 104 808 ¥   shipments after discounts (−8.4%)
lessons.reads: None of the three is wrong: they answer different questions. The gap between the first and second is the retail markup and stock in the channel; between the second and third, distributor discounts. An argument over which is "correct" isn't settled by calculation.
lessons.wrong: "Consolidate the three sources into one warehouse and there'll be a single number"
lessons.wrongWhy: A warehouse doesn't choose between definitions: it will keep all three and add a fourth of its own. A single data mart turns an agreement into code and is therefore useful — but only once the agreement exists. Without one, a technical project simply moves the argument up a level.
lessons.selfCheck: If a meeting spends more than five minutes establishing whose number is right, the problem is no longer in the data. A good outcome for that meeting isn't "we picked a number" but "we assigned a metric owner and a date by which the definition will be written down."
